Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say anything this afternoon, but in view of the previous speaker opening up this subject I feel I must put forward a few of my own ideas and the ideas of hundreds of thousands of men in this country who are associated with me in a great organization. During the past week I had an opportunity to attend as a delegate at Saskatoon the Canadian Legion convention, a convention composed of approximately one thousand men who volunteered their services to defend this country. This organization has a right to be and is very much concerned about immigration; a question of national importance. Because of that, Mr. Speaker, this organization has had a committee on immigration for some years. In 1946 this matter came before the dominion convention, but because of the fact that hundreds of thousands of veterans had to be re-established under after-war conditions, the Canadian Legion took the stand that large-scale immigration was not desirable; but now, owing to the fact that greater numbers of our men are re-established and conditions in this country have changed, that policy was changed by unanimous consent at the convention which I recently had the honour to attend.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Before the house rose at six o'clock, I had just started to bring to its attention the immigration policy proposed and suggested by the Canadian Legion. As I mentioned previously, it is an organization of some
300,000	or more veterans who served this country in war and who are anxious to serve it in peace. It is an organization that represents veterans in all provinces and the majority of racial stocks. Because it wishes to servo this country in peace, it gives serious consideration to national problems that are concerning the Canadian people as a whole. Therefore I wish to bring to the attention of this house the considered and unanimous opinion of the Canadian Legion as expressed at the recent convention held in Saskatoon.
I must say, before proceeding, that I fully realize the difficulties which surround this subject, particularly for the Canadian government. It is complicated, complex and presents difficulties that are not seen by the man in the street. But I suggest that the recommenda-

tions of the Canadian Legion offer a firm basis upon which to build an immigration policy that will receive the support of the majority of the Canadian people.
The committee that dealt with this question was appointed by the legion at the 1946 dominion convention in Quebec. It was a committee made up of some of the most responsible gentlemen in this country, and they gave a great deal of study to the question, considered it from all aspects in view of the rights and interests of Canadians at present resident in Canada and the necessities of Canada for the future.
The over-all tenor of the resolutions submitted to the committee clearly indicates that since the Quebec convention two major factors have been established.
As I previously stated, at the Quebec convention the legion was of the opinion that large-scale immigration was not desirable until the veterans were re-established and conditions had become more stable in this country. Now the legion suggests:
First-that the veterans of the second world war have been re-established to the point where it may now be considered to be in the national interest that immigration should be contemplated on a larger scale; and1
Second-That in connection with the over-all rehabilitation of Europe, Canada must assume her fair share, through immigration, in solving the problem of the displaced person.
I am now reading from the report of the committee on immigration adopted unanimously by that convention:
In connection with the immigration of displaced persons, it is the belief of the committee that, while Canada should stand prepared to do its fair share, the basic desire of Canadians is that the major proportion of new immigrants should be of British and kindred stock, and that immigration activities should be designed to that end.
Then in this report there is reference to the committee's receiving many resolutions in connection with the bringing of immigrants to this country, shall we say, by a process of indentured labour, and strong objection taken to a procedure of immigration which might develop and cause immigrants to be formed into pools of cheap labour. Strong objection was taken to that by many branches of the Canadian Legion; but, owing to the statutory conditions being changed, no action was taken to express an opinion in that respect at the convention. I am sure, however, it is the considered opinion of the legion that they could not support that type of immigration policy. I shall deal briefly with the policy, because I do not wish to take up the time

British Immigration
of the house more than is necessary. I am now again reading from the policy of the Canadian Legion on immigration:
The Canadian Legion is of the opinion that entry into Canada of considerable numbers of immigrants is desirable and should be encouraged, subject to rigid control and supervision. This opinion is based on the following premises:
(a)	Increased population would reduce the per capita cost of governmental and other services;
(b)	Canada is one of the richest, but one of the most under-populated countries in the world. No other country in the temperate zone has such a great wealth of undeveloped natural resources.
(c)	An increase in population is necessary to strengthen Canada's position in national defence;
(d)	Increased population is necessary to maintain our industrial capacity which so greatly expanded during the war, and we must have increased consumption at home for the products of our fields, mines, forests and factories, as well as to enlarge our export markets;
(e)	There is no pioneer or basic labour available in Canada, which is so necessary for the development of our natural resources;
(f)	The legion places strong emphasis on maintaining a favourable balance of British emigrants but appreciates the necessity ot assisting to the utmost the problem of absorbing suitable displaced persons m Europe, now the responsibility of the united nations; provided that adequate measures are taken to avoid embracing in such movements of displaced persons any with a philosophy or ideal alien to our free democratic -way of life. It is believed that persons with special skill or cratt entering Canada from displaced persons camps will enhance our economy by introducing new industries. which ir. turn will provide further opportunities for employment of our citizens. This has already become evident.
And finally:
(h)	The legion considers that with the enlarged importance of immigration it is now time to restore the establishment of a separate and well-organized department under a federal minister concerned only with immigration and settlement, instead of permitting immigration *o continue as a somewhat obscure branch ot the Department of Mines and Resources which has a multiplicity of other unrelated problems to deal with.
I think that is a sound program so far as immigration is concerned.
I wish to deal briefly with the question of displaced persons and of British immigration before resuming my seat. The question of displaced persons is receiving a great deal of consideration from people all across Canada. I am quite sure that the majority of the Canadian people are anxious that we shall play our part in bringing desirable displaced persons to this country. But there is a certain feeling of uneasiness as to the type of some of these displaced persons who are coming to this country, with regard to whether they are suitable people or are receiving suitable location and so on. I might say that, from my conversation with some representatives of organized labour, I find considerable uneasiness in this connection. Only recently I had a letter from the mother of a girl who served with the women's auxiliary corps during this war and who wished to enter domestic service. She did not secure the position because a displaced person offered to take the job at a lower rate of pay. These things are concerning organized labour. I think the government must pay strict attention to that sort of thing and see to it that these people who are brought into this country are not exploited because of their ignorance of conditions, and their natural desire, shall I say, to do something to express their appreciation of being allowed to come to Canada.
I might also say, Mr. Speaker, that the veterans are concerned about this problem. I have talked to a good number of veterans and I find many of them seriously concerned. When I was proceeding to the convention at Saskatoon there were two carloads of displaced persons on the train on which we were riding, and with a number of veterans-and incidentally some from the province of Quebec -I made a tour of those coaches. The least I can say in that respect is that we were not impressed with what we saw.
Quite recently I had occasion to have a conversation on this matter with an official of another government from Germany; and as a result, I would say the Canadian government has been too late in acting to secure the best type of displaced person to bring to Canada. From the information I received, it is my opinion that many of the best of these people have gone to other countries. I am all in favour of bringing to Canada the relatives of good citizens of this country. They can be provided with homes; they have contacts which will enable them to obtain jobs. I am all in favour of bringing those we are certain were on our side during the last war, who were willing to go to concentration camps for the sake of their principles, and who suffered. I know there are those who for political reasons, cannot return to certain European countries, but any man who is a political refugee and also a sound democrat should be able to come to this country.
At the same time, from what I hear, I am of the opinion our screening of these people is not entirely satisfactory. In making this criticism I fully realize the difficulties. We want to be certain that the people we bring here are those tvho will accept and develop.
British Immigration

our democratic ideals and our attitude toward life. We also want to make sure that when they come to this country they are not going to displace a veteran or another Canadian from a home, but that they will be able to find homes and employment, and can be properly absorbed.
Reference was made by the speaker who preceded me to the fact that a great many of these people are very suitable to go on the land, and I have no doubt that is true. Personally, however, I do not think we should take such a pessimistic view of Canadian youth as to suggest that they all wish to go to the cities. This government, and other governments in this country, must put forth a greater effort to make rural life attractive to young Canadian men and women. To me it is deplorable to see the sons of the pioneers who built this country leaving the farms and going to the cities. Why are they doing that? In many cases it is because rural life is not on a par with urban life as far as certain conveniences, remuneration and rewards are concerned. I believe we have to remedy that situation, if we are going to keep young Canadians at farming.
I want now to say just a word or two concerning British immigration; naturally, as an Englishman born, this subject is very dear to my heart. During the last two sessions I have been interested in reading the minutes of the committee on immigration of what I think is officially termed in this house "the other place." During those two whole sessions I challenge anyone to show that more than five minutes have been given to a discussion of British immigration. I think that is out of all proportion. It may be said that thousands of British people have been brought to this country, but if you take out of that total the wives and dependents of veterans who married overseas you will find that a very small number indeed of Britishers have been brought to this country since the conclusion of the war.
I brought up this matter previously in the house, and at that time the minister said the British people were welcome to this country.
I believe that is so; if they can pass the health tests and comply with all the regulations, they may come here. But that is not sufficient when we have in Britain over 180,000 ex-service men who stood side by side with us, who fought for us and who stand for the same type of civilization, dasiring to come to this country.
Therefore I believe that if this country is to have a balanced immigration policy, as between displaced persons and British and

kindred people, this government must give consideration to making arrangements for transportation for those people. They do not want charity; they do not want their fares paid. All they ask and all the legion asks of this government is that something be done to provide shipping, so that they may pay their fares and come to this country in the near future. I remember in the early days of this century seeing many British immigrants of the type generally known as cockneys, a fine people, arriving, at Halifax and Montreal. They were not met by committees of ladies with buns and hot coffee and popcorn and all the rest of it. They had their baggage on their shoulders, got into colonist cars and went to western Canada on their own, where they made a great contribution to the development of this country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I do ask this government" to	give	consideration to	taking

Mr. Speaker, before Your Honour leaves the chair, I should like to make a brief statement. On	February 25 of	this year, as recordedin Hansard at page 1621, I read to the house the following quotation from the report of the	committee	on	evangelism and	social
service of the United Church of Canada:
We are driven to the conclusion that the only thing that will solve our present day social and economic problems will he the absolute Christian socialization of the means of production and distribution of all the necessities of life.
I went on to say it was no wonder church bodies took this position, and I repeated the quotation I have just read. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) then interjected with this question: "Does that include the farmers?" In keeping with the view of the United Church which I was then quoting, I quite naturally replied: "That would include everybody." It is perfectly clear that in my reply to the hon. m.ember for Peel I expressed the belief that the views of the United Church applied to everyone. After all, the church believes that Christianity is for all, including the farmers, of whom I am one.
However I regret to say that this statement has been widely distorted outside this house

by people who know better. In many newspaper editorials and advertisements it is being alleged that my remark means that the C.C.F. proposes to socialize farm lands. Mr. Speaker, what I am about to say I had intended to say during the debate on the budget. In order to expedite the taking of the vote last Thursday evening, I agreed to defer my remarks until a motion for the house to go into committee; otherwise I would have spoken on the budget.
Tonight I wish to discuss a situation which I think is dangerous, and becoming more dangerous. I refer to the zionist-communist propaganda which is general not only in the United States but in Canada, and which is strongly anti-British. I refer particularly, of course, to the Palestine question. I am not going to discuss the actual conditions in Palestine itself; that matter does not concern me at the present time. What I am concerned about is how the war between the Zionists and the Arabs is extending outside, or is likely to extend outside beyond the boundaries of Palestine and to bring about-indeed it is bringing about-a great deal of ill-feeling and hostility among nations which otherwise w'ould be friendly and together.
In fact, if one reads the propaganda or listens to the radio, and statements made, one might believe that Great Britain is a foreign country. Canadians are being told to regard Great Britain, and those countries which agree with her foreign policies, as enemy countries.
According to the press, zionist high command have appealed to Russia for assistance not only against the Arabs but against Great Britain and the Arabs. That is the statement which appeared in Saturday's, press. Let me quote first
of all a British statement dated at London, May 22. which says:
Britain was reported reliably today to have told the United States preservation of Arab friendship is essential to safeguard the middle east against the march of communism.
Again it says that the United States ambassador saw Mr. Bevin and discussed the situation, and continues:-
Though official sources refused formal comment, it was learned British officials here and in Washington have told the United States Arab-Brutish relations must be maintained as a "great barrier against the flow of communism to the south."
Taking that as a basis, which I do-I accept it as the soundest statement that can be made on the subject-it now appears that in the united nations organization Russia and the United States are lined up against Great Britain. That is the situation which has arisen as a consequence of Palestine policy.
I should like to read this statement by Sir Ellsworth Flavelle which was printed last week in the press:
At this point I wish to state as a warning my profound conviction concerning the Irgunists and Sternists. My feeling is shared by my colleagues of the world committee and of the Canadian Palestine committee. The future prestige. welfare and indeed survival of this modern Jewish state depends upon the success of its government in eliminating from the Palestiniai: Jewish community the activities of these terrorists whose operations as gunmen and assassins have been deplored and condemned by all civilized peoples.
Failure to suppress these terrorists will alienate opinion and support from the Jewish state among men of good will throughout the world, and. through them, the support of their governments.
That may be the opinion of Sir Ellsworth Flavelle, but that is certainly not a true picture so far as the situation is concerned, because these terrorists operate not only or even mainly in Palestine, but outside as well. And all those people of good will who have seen the danger of the situation for several years and who have done their level best to inform and to warn the Canadian people-not only the Canadian people but the American people and the British people-as to its dangers; those of us who have tried to inform public opinion of the dangers we saw so clearly have come under the same terrorist organization as British soldiers and officials in Palestine itself. I shall give proof of that before I take my seat.
Then Sir Ellsworth Flavelle says:
All the world knows that the UNO are giving final form and substance to the best legal and moral judgment of united nations.

That also I shall show is not the opinion of everybody by any means. It is all very well to say that we condemn the methods of these terrorists, but what has been done effectively?
Has anything effective been tried to put a stop to them?
Let me quote from an advertisement in the United States paper freely sold and circulated throughout Canada, from one side to the other. I refer to the New York paper PM. It states:
For the British the situation in Palestine deteriorated only when the Arabs began to run. Hagarni and Irgun took over Haifa. Irgun pushed into Jaffa, took Manshiyeh quarter and turned it over to Hagana. The Arab-nazi gangsters were thrown into panic. The Arabs began to run like rats. The British were shocked. They had expected the Arab-nazi stooges and pimps to slaughter "the Jews". By that time they expected to be well out of Palestine. Then Bevin could look the world in the eye and say: "Who, me? We weren't even there. Can we help it if the Arabs and Jews kill each other?"
I say that sort of propaganda is absolutely unfair and it is a menace to world peace. It states further:
Sanctimoniously the British will say, or are already saying, that they are sending their troops back to reinforce the truce to serve the U.N. Our state department-
That is the United States state department.
-is exerting itself to help foster this lie. It is a lie. The only truce the British will support in Palestine is a devil's truce designed to wipe out the Hebrews.
It is hardly necessary for me to mention the zionist intimidation and terrorism, the sending of bombs and of letters threatening death, the different methods which have been carried out in more than one instance even at the risk of innocent people being murdered. In contrast to this, I should like to quote a news release by the Canadian Arab news service which I, along with other members of the house, received last week. This is issued by Mr. Massoud, who I believe is president of the Canadian Arab friendship league:
"The hatred and propaganda dispensed by some high-pressure groups of this country and the United States has resulted in the present slaughter of thousands of innocent people in the Holy Land. Our warnings of the past five years and our appeals to the Jewish people and their fanatical supporters have not been heeded. Now that Arabs are fighting and defending their homes and while the battle is about to gain momentum, we are again appealing to all those responsible, including the members of the various governments who favoured partition of the Holy Land, to realize the implication of their action of the past.
"The Canadian Arab friendship league," Mr. Massoud said, "will have no part in the fighting. We are firstly Canadian citizens and, as such,

have done our duty when we worked for peace in the Holy Land. We also know that none of the Arab countries now engaged in the struggle would ask for our military assistance. There will be no maple leaf battalion fighting on the side of the Arabs, no matter how many similar groups may be recruited by the News."
I quote that to show the difference in the spirit of the two sides. It cannot be said that these things are being done only by groups like the Irgun and other so-called terrorist organizations because, as I said before, no effort has been made by the high command to suppress these people. In fact the terrorist groups are in the van leading the zionist troops. It was stated officially by these zionist terrorists that any British who were caught or captured in the war would be shot as criminals. I wonder what the reaction would have been in Canada if that threat had been made by the Arabs against the late "Buzz" Beurling. Had "Buzz" Beurling been fortunate enough to have survived and unfortunate enough to have been captured in Palestine, I have no doubt he would have been treated by the Arabs as an honourable prisoner of war. There again is the difference in the spirit of the two sides. That difference is not confined to Palestine; it extends outside Palestine.
I mentioned zionist propaganda and their control of the radio and the press. From time to time I have made radio broadcasts based on speeches I had made in this house in an effort to throw some light on a dangerous situation. One broadcast was simply suppressed; not one word was put on the air, though I knew nothing of it until afterward. The last broadcast of a few weeks ago was censored. I shall not mention the name of the station or of the manager, because I do not think that would be fair.
I do not hold this manager responsible, because he is in fear of this same terrorist organization. That is quite obvious from what he said when he objected to certain statements which I had made in my broadcast.
In particular, I find in your speech such statements as, page 5, "And so it is with Zionism: All Zionists may not be communists, but all communists and fellow-travelling socialists back zionism."
That is a fair statement and I make it without fear of successful contradiction. Then I mentioned that Henry Morgenthau is an international financier and zionist. I had to cross out the words "and zionist" for the same reason. Another statement to which he objected was:
In my speech I was glad to pay my humble tribute to the British soldiers and policemen in Palestine who through all these years have borne the brunt of savage zionist gangsterism.

Palestine
More than 300 British soldiers and policemen in Palestine have been murdered in cold blood by these same zionist organizations, but I was not to be allowed to pay that tribute over the radio to our own kith and kin. The station manager went on to say:
Within the listening area of this station there are many Jews of the highest probity and reputation-some of our best and most substantial citizens are of that race. I cannot think that it is in the public interest, nor that it is fair, for them and their race to be maligned and attacked.
In other words, I might hurt the feelings of these fine gentlemen by expressing my sympathy for the 300 British men, our kith and kin. who were murdered in Palestine by Zionists.

And in a Canadian
broadcast.

Have those fine citizens ever raised their voices against these murderers? If they have I have never heard them. Have they ever come out and publicly condemned the terrorists in Palestine? If they have I have never heard them. I have every sympathy with the manager of this station because I know the power of this organization. He goes on to say:
I do not think that my obligation as the licensee of the station compels me to carry speeches containing quotations such as those outlined in the quotations given.
Everybody knows today that radio is one of the greatest means of expressing public opinion. We are told that if we are to preserve our freedom we must preserve the freedom of the press at all costs. But when you want to deal with political Zionism there is no freedom in the press or on the radio, as I shall prove.
I might mention, and here I am betraying no secrets because it was made public at the time, last December, the editor of the paper run by the movement of which I am a member published a statement which I put on Hansard the last time I spoke, and as a result of my attempts to warn the country of the danger of this situation, the Canadian Zionist League-this is their statement., not mine-forced the resignation of the two editors of the Canadian Social Crediter, because of its anti-Semitism, and it went on to say that the one chiefly affected would be Norman Jaques.
I have said it until I am tired of saying it, that to criticize political zionism is no more anti-Semitic than it would be for a Tory to criticize a socialist or a socialist a Tory. But even if it were anti-Semitic, let me point out, that recently a case went to the high court in
Great Britain in which an editor had in an editorial in his paper given vent to his feelings as a result of the outrages against his own countrymen in Palestine, and he was sued for seditious libel. That case attracted worldwide attention. It did not get too much publicity in this country; but I took the trouble to send for the evidence which I have here word for word. I am not a lawyer, of course, and I am only quoting counsel for the defence. Counsel for the defence said that subject to the ruling of the court, a man had as much right to criticize the Jews as he had to criticize anybody else. The judge, Mr. Justice Birkett, in summing up told the jury that the most vital aspect of the case was the preservation of the freedom of speech; that it was of the utmost importance that nothing should be done by the court which could in any way impair or injure freedom of speech and freedom of the press. Yet, as I say, with regard to the Palestine question, neither in the press nor on the radio in this country has one been free to make full statements other than for the zionist cause.
I might, quote two members of congress. Speaking in the house of representatives on December 18, 1947, the Hon. Lawrence Smith said:
Let us take a look at the record, Mr. Speaker, and see what happened in the united nations assembly meeting prior to the vote on partition. A two-thirds vote was required to pass the resolution. On two occasions the assembly was to vote and twice it was postponed. It was obvious that the delay was necessary because the proponents did not have the necessary votes. In the meantime, it is reliably reported that intense pressure was applied to the delegates of three small nations by the United States members and also by officials "at the highest levels in Washington." Now that is a serious charge. When the matter was finally considered on. the 29th-
That would be the 29th of September.
-what happened? The decisive votes for partition were cast by Haiti, Liberia, and the Philippines. These votes were sufficient to make the two-thirds majority. Previously, these countries opposed the move. Do not forget, Mr. Speaker, that they are considered satellites of our own country.
That is of the United States, of course.
The pressure by our delegates, by our officials, and by private citizens of the United States constitutes reprehensible conduct against them and against us . . . Time will tell, and this congress should authorize a full-dress investigation so that the people of this country may know that the united nations has been used in this instance as a vehicle of torture, and not as an instrument of international justice.
The fact is that faith has largely been lost in the united nations, and more on account of
Palestine

this Palestine question than anything else, and today we find that Moscow and New York are lining up against Great Britain. That is the situation which we face today. The people who have advocated political Zionism, which they have a perfect right to do, have gone beyond that and maligned those who have taken the other view and tried to point out the dangers of what they knew must develop. I say that all those people who have banned criticism of political Zionism will now have to rise and testify whether they are on the side of Russian communism or on the side of Canadian democracy and British freedom, or world freedom, for that matter.
I should like to quote another member of the United States Congress. Hon. Edward Gossett, addressing the house of representatives on December 11 last, said:
It seems to me to be ironic and tragic that we should be fighting communism with the one hand and encouraging it with the other. I refer to what seems to me a stupid, if not a criminal, act on the part of our delegation to the united nations in the partition of Palestine and in the delivery of that part of the world to communist influence. By that act alone we have taken a major step toward antagonizing the whole Moslem world . . .
In this Palestine partition we have played petty partisan politics on the very threshold of what should be an American century. We have jeopardized American leadership by such tactics; we may have signed the death knell of the united nations. It seems to me it might be well for the foreign affairs commitee to investigate the part played by American delegates to the united nations. Not only was their action in the partition of Palestine a great disservice to the Jews but it was also a very real service to communism in the far east, the middle east, and in the near east.
It is doubtful that all the money we have spent and will spend in Europe can offset the evil we have done in the rest of the world by our meddling with the Palestine question.
That opinion agrees with the British official statement which I quoted at the beginning of my remarks, in which they said that if communism is to be stopped spreading in the near, the middle and the far east, then we must retain the good will of the Moslem world. As I say, those who have supported the zionist cause, which, of course, they had a right to do, could plead that, up to now they were mistaken; but they cannot say that any longer in the face of the situation as it is today. We have to choose. We have either to make a stand for British, western and world freedom or take our stand in support of world communism. That is the situation, and without being political in the least I make the statement that one reason the communists are supporting the C.C.F. is that the C.C.F. as an 
organization, support and strongly support, have gone out of their way to support, political Zionism. It is a fact that not only the C.C.F., but socialists everywhere support zionism. I do not mean labour when I say socialists. The C.C.F. backed the Zionists and the communists back both. There is no doubt of that.

Do the C.C.F. concur in that?
Mr. JAQUES; I am quite willing to acquit them of any wrong intention. I am quite willing to believe that they did not understand just what they were doing. I am quite willing to give them that credit. I am perfectly sure that the rank and file have not the faintest idea of what it is all about.
You know it all, of course.

time.

If I might add one more
sentence.

speechtext:
Mr. PATRICK H. ASHBY (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of my fellow members of parliament a matter of the utmost importance, namely, the growth of bureaucracy in this country which is completely ignoring the sovereignty of the people, and establishing the supremacy of rules and regulations over their lives. Today the people of Canada are being forced to adjust their 'lives and living to fit into rules and regulations instead of rules and regulations being adjusted to fit their needs and wants. Bureaucracy, or stateism, has reversed the functions for which these bureaux were originally established.
I shall deal briefly with only one department
of the government at this time, taking up only fifteen minutes or so, and that is the department known as the Post Office Department. I have deliberately avoided using the words "the postal services", because the Post Office Department no longer serves the people of Canada,
but is rather using the people as a means of obtaining revenue from which these bureaucrats in control can obtain their livelihood. I should like to quote from a broadcast I delivered some time ago, which outlined somewhat briefly the original functions of the postal services as established:
The postal services were originally established by far-seeing men for a purpose, and that purpose was to carry and deliver the mails to their destination; to carry news and knowledge; to promote mutual acquaintance; to bring the people of our nation closer together and not only the people of our own country, but of all peoples of all the nations who would associate with the postal services of our great British commonwealth of free nations. The postal services were established to bring peace and good will among all men and women no matter what colour or creed. The individuals employed by us in this great service were messengers of sympathy and of love. They carried messages that would console the lonely, that would be a bond holding together scattered members of a family. They carried news from departed friends and loved ones. The postal service in those days used as their motto "service first".
A motto that was apparently not known to the Postmaster General himself when I asked that question some time ago. Today the motto of the Post Office Department is apparently "service last."
In days gone by, the individuals employed in this wonderful service prided themselves on delivering His Majesty's mail if humanly possible. In fact, the first mails ever carried were messages from the king himself, and even to this day the postage stamp bears the likeness of our sovereign and king.
It is the king's mail today as always and refusal to deliver His Majesty's mail is an insult to our king and sovereign as well as to the sovereign people of Canada; for our king does not represent party politics, but the people of our great British commonwealth- all the people. That is why I say the people are sovereign in this country, not these hired bureaucrats nor their paid elected representatives who are sitting in this house today.
The people of Canada do not live in this country to serve this institution-the Post Office Department-or any other institution. All these institutions were created for no other purpose than to serve the sovereign people.
I should like now to quote from an early bulletin issued by the Post Office Department:
The post office opens up new territory in advance of the railways. As soon as a trail is blazed-*
Not paved or gravelled sidewalks and streets, let it be remembered.
-and settlers break new land for a home in the wilderness, the post office links up the new community with the other parts of the country.

Postal Service-Edmonton District
In Rudyard Kipling's verses "The Overland Mail", he pays tribute to the carriers of the oeople's mail in these words:
Is the torrent in spate? He must ford it or swim.
Has the rain wrecked the road? He must climb by the cliff.
Docs the tempest cry halt? What are tempests to him?
The service admits not a "but" or an "if".
While the breath's in his mouth, he must bear without fail.
In the name of the Empress, the Overland Mail.
In those days, unfortunately of long ago, the postal services prided themselves, and rightly so, on visiting with kindly friendship and service every fireside. They mingled with the throbbings of almost every heart in our great British commonwealth of free nations. They administered to all the varied climates of our vast empire, from the far northern outposts amidst snow and perpetual ice to the steaming jungles of the tropics, with the same eagerness to serve the sovereign peoples. His Majesty's mail was delivered to its destination, and like a delicate stethoscope held to trusting ears, families and isolated individuals and even whole nations whispered their joys and their sorrows, their convictions and sympathetic understandings to each other though separated by thousands of miles of prairie or mountain ranges.
Now let us compare those wonderful services rendered by this institution years ago with the services they are rendering today. I should like to show hon. members the photograph of a postman delivering the mails in the city of Edmonton this spring, not in any particular area, but one of the many wearing rubber boots and tramping through the water. This was postman Wes. Ferry who braved the elements to deliver the mail. During the year January 1, 1947, to January 1, 1948

that is 365 full days-there were only eleven days when postmen had need to wear rubbers to deliver the mail in the Grierson estate area-in which are living 125 families of our veterans who purchased their homes through the D.V.A.-in order, of course to keep the boots of the postman free from mud. All winter long the ordinary footwear was sufficient to enable the postman to carry out his duties. Only during muddy conditions would he have need to wear rubbers; then only on eleven days had this condition existed, and even then he could have walked on the grass instead of on the rough gravel.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house another postman, named Alfred Forrest of Edmonton, who served the people faithfully for thirty-eight years. This is what

he had to say when he was told that the Post Office Department refused to deliver mail to these veterans and insisted upon concrete sidewalks:
Sidewalks indeed. I once had to build a raft to deliver mail on my route in the Norwood district of this city of Edmonton. The mail had to get through-
Remember that was the motto of days gone by.
[DOT]-so I hunted around, found some planks, lashed them together and made my raft. I slung my mail pouch over my shoulder, grabbed a pole and put out to sea. I delivered every letter as usual although I had to punt from door to door.
That was during the pioneer days of years gone by when the motto of the postal service was "service first," and mighty proud were the postmen of those days to wear the badge of the postal service and mighty proud were we of our sons and parents who delivered the mails.
I have here another photograph of a fourteen-year-old boy, named Terry Stubbert, of the city of Edmonton who volunteered to carry His Majesty's mails to each of these homes, along with the daily newspaper, the Edmonton Bulletin. This boy has delivered the Edmonton Bulletin regularly to these homes ever since they were first inhabited. They get all the services from private institutions. Laundry is picked up and delivered; groceries are delivered. Every service is rendered except that by a government controlled institution which forces these people to pay for these services and then refuses to render them.

speechtext: Hurrah for free enterprise!

speechtext:
That is right; that is what we want, free enterprise. I will guarantee that if the postal services were run as a free enterprise, in competition, postal rates would immediately be reduced fifty per cent and a better service would be given. I want to quote a letter from the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) himself, dated February 14, 1948, in which he says:
Governmental policy for the coming fiscal year calls for the reduction of controllable expenditures to the absolute minimum and for the postponement wherever possible of the introduction of new services and enlargement of existing ones. This means that no letter carrier services can be granted and that extensions oi delivery beyond existing boundaries will have to be withheld, except where the need is most urgent and where conditions are ideal.
In other words, the Post Office Department admits its failure to render efficient service to the people who now pay fully twice as much for these services as they have ever paid in the past.
Of course it is always easy to criticize, I know, and I sometimes hesitate to do so; but

Postal Service-Edmonton District
this is such a glaring instance of inefficiency, and I think I can say bureaucratic bungling, that I must bring it to the attention of hon. members. I sent a telegram to the Postmaster General last March. When I left Edmonton on April 1 no acknowledgement of that telegram had been received. When I arrived in Ottawa I got in touch with the Postmaster General, reminding him that I had received no reply to this telegram, and he assured me he would reply to it, which apparently he did immediately. But instead of sending the letter from his office to my office, a matter of a few yards, the letter was actually addressed to me at box 34, rural route No. 3, South Edmonton, Alberta; and it was mailed on April 5, the very day I was in my place in this house. Apparently they did not even know parliament was in session. This letter was carried thousands of miles to my home, where it was delayed a week because of the condition of the roads. My family could not get back into town to forward the letter. Then again it travelled thousands of miles back to me here, in order to be delivered a few yards from the office from *which it was originally mailed.
In this letter the Postmaster General states that the rules and regulations must be obeyed. He says first the householder must do his part. He must have a letter slot in his door; the house must be numbered, and there must be a sidewalk from the door to the street. Then the community must provide suitable walks and roads; the streets must be named, and so on. When all these conditions are fulfilled and ideal, then and not until then will the Post Office Department give the matter consideration.
You see, Mr. Speaker, the whole thing has been thrown into reverse. That is why one day I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself to tell us why members were originally elected by the people to assemble in parliament. The purpose was to prevent forced taxation of the people; and until we reverse the present process and abolish all forced taxation we shall gradually drift into dictatorship. Bureaucracy, of course, is the first step toward dictatorship.
The situation in the Grierson estate is this. We have 125 houses occupied by veterans and their families, all within the city limits of Edmonton, with no vacant space between this area and the old, established mail delivery routes. In other words, mail is delivered on the east, the west and the south. It is delivered on one side of the street, but not on the other side. In fact one family told me their mail was delivered at the front door but the mail man would not drop the mail of another family
living at the back, even though he had to walk right past the door, because it was not supposed to be on his route.
All services are rendered by free enterprise without taxation; let us remember that. No one taxes these people for these services which are rendered voluntarily by free enterprise. There is no forced payment of any kind. But the Post Office Department forces these veterans to pay through taxation for this service which is not being rendered to them.
I saw the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) about this matter, and he asssured me his department would do all they could. I believe he has done so. I know he is extremely busy, but he has co-operated with the city of Edmonton, and his department has undertaken to pay $2,700 toward the cost of graveling these roads. The city of Edmonton will pay up to $2,550; but, since $7,800 is required, the sum of $2,550 is still lacking, and the sidewalks will not be built until that amount is forthcoming. Where is that money to come from? We cannot blame these veterans; they have done their part. They were willing to go overseas and fight. They did not ask for paved sidewalks, or even umbrellas. They left their homes, their business, their education. They made every sacrifice in order that we might be preserved as a free country. When they came back they looked forward to this wonderful new social order they were promised. These homes were not given to them. They had to buy and pay for them at high cost, plus interest. Now they find they are not to be given postal service. We cannot blame them. We cannot blame the postmen, the sorters and others in the Post Office Department. They are all loyal workers and many have volunteered to deliver mail to this very area. As a matter of fact, the department has discharged men from the Edmonton post office since the war, claiming they were not required. These men begged me to help them remain in the service. They liked the work and wanted to remain there. They were quite willing to deliver mail in this area, but their request was refused.
So we cannot blame the postmen. Nor can we blame the people of Canada, who have done all they possibly could. I do not think we can blame the bureaucrats, the higher-ups, because they tell me, "We are merely carrying out the rules and regulations laid down by you people in parliament." Therefore the only people we can blame are ourselves, who have permitted these rules and regulations to be introduced into this house and passed. Therefore, since you and I are to blame, we should pay for this extra service, which would mean but a matter of $10 each.

Veterans Land Act-Saskatchewan
So, on behalf of the returned soldiers of this country I am assessing each member of the house the sum of $10. We get $4,000 a year plus $2,000, tax free, which we voted for ourselves; and it is nothing but fair and just that we should do so. Therefore in my hat I place my $10, and I shall go around and collect it from the other members.

maintopic: VETERANS LAND ACT-ADMINISTRATION, SASKATCHEWAN-REFUGEES AND DISPLACED PERSONS
VETERANS LAND ACT-ADMINISTRATION, SASKATCHEWAN-REFUGEES AND DISPLACED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member has not carried out his threat to call on all of us.
Before Your Honour leaves the chair, there is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the house, namely the administration of the Veterans Land Act. During the period of the last two or three years I have had occasion, on more than one visit among my constituents, to hear complaints made in respect of the administration of the act. Within the last three or four months a change has taken place in the directorship. It is now presided over by Brigadier Rutherford who, in March last, in accepting the new position said that many of the anomalies in connection with the administration of the act would be removed. He pointed out particularly the necessity for an improvement in public relations. Among other things he stated that, in the administration of the act, he intended that the officials should

and I use his own words-"Never forget that they are servants of the veteran and of the public".
During the past two or three years on more than one occasion I have raised strenuous objection to the fact that, in settling individual veterans under the act, in too many instanaes areas within the province of Saskatchewan were being discriminated against. I very well realize that the objection taken by the administration in connection with new settlers going into certain of these areas might be justifiable. But in too many cases veterans who have returned to the areas in which they were raised have been denied the opportunity of settlement there. On a number of occasions I have brought these matters to the attention of the department, and I feel that, conditions not having improved or changed, the time has now come to bring the matter to the attention of the house.

I am not going to speak at great length this evening, but in support of my contention that in the administration of the act discrimination has been practised as against certain areas, I point out that various areas in my own constituency have regularly been denied settlement by soldier settlers desirous of maintaining themselves adjacent to their parents' farms.
Then, too, in addition to the fact that there has been discrimination, one has no opportunity to find out the reasons why settlement is denied; for whenever an individual asks why he is denied settlement in an area, or why his application has not been accepted, the answer in every case by the department has been similar to the one I now have before me, as follows:
We regret to advise that our opinion of this farm must he treated as strictly confidential; and we are therefore unable to set out the reasons for declining.
I say that is unfair. When a decision is made against a veteran who desires to settle in a given area, the veteran should at least be entitled to the reasons why he has been denied the right to settle in the area where he believes he could make good. I would ask that this discrimination against certain areas in the province be removed, so far as veterans living in those areas and who are desirous of settling there are concerned.
My second objection to the present administration is that it is dilatory in its decisions. Veterans have to wait too long in too many instances for decisions regarding their applications. To show the effect of that, I would refer to one case only where a soldier settler intending to settle on land applied in 1946, and on January 14, 1948, received word that his application had finally been accepted. He also applied to purchase certain machinery. During the period between the time he made his application and the decision was rendered by the board, the machinery required for his purposes had materially increased in price. In 1946, when his application was made the price of an Oliver 70 tractor was $1,258; and by the time his application was decided the price of the tractor had gone up to $1772.25, or an increase of $487. He also required a 10-foot Oliver combine. At the time his application was made that combine could be procured for $1,460.90, but by the time the decision was made the cost had gone up to $2,046. Surely delays such as that should not be permitted.
I realize the minister is not here at the moment, but I am suggesting that he make a full investigation of the situation with a view to removing those anomalies.

Veterans Land Act-Saskatchewan
Then, too, I would place before the house the request of one branch of the legion in Saskatchewan-and it is generally approved now-that the amount of Veterans' Land Act grants and loans should be materially increased. I have before me in that connection a resolution passed by the Go van branch of the Canadian Legion, which summarizes the viewpoint generally held in that regard. Instead of enlarging upon it, I shall merely place the resolution upon record. It states:
That the dominion government be asked to increase the V.L.A. grants and loans to veteran farmers so that the amount of the grant or loan will have the same purchasing power today as the grant or loan to the veteran farmer had in September, 1945.
It points out increases which have taken place in prices of commodities the veteran has to buy. It points out that if there is to be reasonable equality as between veterans who today settle on the land and those who settled in September, 1945, there should be a material increase.
I pointed out discrimination against the prairies, and in that connection I have here a number of resolutions passed in various parts of the prairie provinces asking why it is that in their areas this is being practised. I pointed out instances of dilatoriness which I think are inexcusable. Then I want to refer to some of the arbitrary regulations which have been passed and which pare down the rights of the veteran under this act.
We in this house so often find ourselves in the position of passing an act which is generous in its application and then, because of regulations, we discover that the rights which flow from that act are greatly pared down by departmental officials. Prior to 1936, when regulations were to be passed under an act the act invariably contained these words or words to the same effect, "The regulations shall not increase or detract from the powers contained in the act." It is different today when we so often give the power to the governor in council or to officials to pass regulations uncontrolled in their application.
Under this act there are too many cases of regulations being passed which deny that fair and generous interpretation which the act should provide. I want to point out an instance of what I believe is an arbitrary attitude adopted by the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. I shall take the specific case of a number of veterans in Prince Albert who built houses on small urban holdings for which the act provides. They moved into their houses early in 1946. Each had been given a definite final price and they were promised certain further improvements.
After they had taken possession, they were advised that the price which had been quoted to them was incorrect and that a larger price would have to be paid, the increase being approximately S400. One man had actually signed an agreement for $5,575. He had made his monthly payments, but he was asked to return the agreement he had signed and to execute a new one for $6,020. That happened in eight cases in Prince Albert.
The veterans were advised that, unless they paid the larger price, they would have to vacate their premises. I say that is unfair and unjustified. Finally the one who had signed an agreement refused to sign another agreement. He had certain grants and allowances coming to him, and he received a notice from the departmental officials that unless he paid the larger price, unless he returned the agreement he had already executed and entered into another agreement for the price then asked by the department, he would be denied the allowances to which he was entitled. These are some of the reasons why I believe an investigation should be made even at this time into the administration of the Veterans' Land Act to the end that any injustice may be remedied.
I should like to see provision made for closer co-operation between the administration of the Veterans' Land Act and veterans in connection with providing machinery and the like. I found that when Mr. Mackenzie was minister and these matters were brought to his attention he invariably endeavoured to do what was humanly possible in order to assure a proper and necessary supply of the machinery required by the veteran. I realize the difficulties, but some provision should be made for priority of machinery, in particular priority of combines and the like when the present harvest season comes around.
I referred a moment ago to how regulations detract from the working out of the act, and I have here an example of an unjust interpretation of a regulation. The Veterans' Land Act provides an opportunity for veterans to take up land. I have before me the record of a veteran whose total disability was ruled in January last to be five per cent. Prior to his enlistment, this man had been a farmer, but he was turned down under the act on the ground that his physical condition would deny re-establishment as a farmer.
These are a few of the things which have caused injustice, which have caused unfairness and which have caused many veterans to believe that the administration of the act has not been as generous as the parliament of Canada intended it to be. I am not going to

say any more at this time, but I ask the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, to review the situation in the prairie provinces generally and in Saskatchewan in particular, in order to remove the discrimination that is being exercised today against individuals who wish to settle in the areas in which they were raised, to the end that delays will be done away with as far as possible, that dilatoriness will be considered inexcusable in connection with matters such as this, that regulations will be widened rather than restricted as at the present time and that the provisions of the act will be carried out in accordance with the desires of parliament and the welfare of the veterans in general.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss briefly a matter which -was raised earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. ETerridge). I believe the house will agree that the provision of sanctuary to refugees is one of the oldest international institutions we know of. I have been looking around for a good definition of "refugee". I came across a little pamphlet written by John Hope Simpson, a gentleman who has been most intimately connected with refugee work from 1926 to 1933. His definition of "refugee" is as follows:
A "refugee" might be described as an involuntary migrant. He would rather remain where he is, but conditions religious, economic, political, or social have rendered his life there so uncomfortable or, indeed, so unbearable, that he is forced to migrate from his home and to search for more tolerable conditions of life elsew-here.
On the basis of that, I believe Canada has a definite responsibility to give sanctuary and help to refugees, regardless of whether they may be political, religious or any other sort of refugee. Aside from the more formal commitments we have made as a member of the united nations and as a participant in the international refugee organization, we have a moral responsibility, which I think is set out very well in the draft declaration of human rights which has been before the committee dealing with human rights and fundamental freedoms, and has found pretty general agreement among those who participated. I should like to quote from the second paragraph of article 10 of the draft declaration on human rights:
Individuals shall have the right to leave their own country and, if they so desire, to acquire the nationality of any country willing to grant it_
Article 11 reads:
Every one shall have the right to seek and be granted asylum from persecution. This right

will not be accorded to criminals nor to those whose acts are contrary to the principles and
aims of the united nations.
I think on the basis of the definition I have given of "refugee" and the draft declaration I have just quoted, we in this country, regardless of where we sit in this house, can subscribe to the sentiments expressed in that declaration and to the commitment that Canada has entered into in promising to do her share in providing a sanctuary for refugees and displaced persons.
Since some question might arise concerning the attitude of organized labour in this country toward the entry of displaced persons, I should like to quote from the evidence given by Mr. Mosher, president of the Canadian Congress of Labour, before the standing committee on immigration and labour in July, 1946. Speaking on behalf of the congress, he said:
The admission of refugees, though it has, of course, economic aspects, is primarily a humanitarian question. Canada is under an obligation to humanity to admit her due share of refugees even if it costs her something. It may actually bring her important economic benefits. But even it it does not, she must do her part.
That is the official attitude of the Canadian Congress of Labour. I should also like to quote a paragraph from a brief submitted by the Ukrainian Catholic Council, and endorsed by the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Diocese of Canada:
It is desirous that the dominion government, at the least, arrange for the immigration of the refugees who already have affidavits from their Canadian next-of-kin, and for whose transportation and welfare guarantees have been made by these Canadian citizens.
Lastly I want to quote from a speech by my own leader in this house on March 29, 1946, a passage which met with general agreement on all sides of the house:
Displaced persons or refugees who are [DOT] relatives of persons living in Great Britain are permitted to enter upon request being made and certain assurances being given by those persons in Great Britain. It seems to ine that if the British^ people with their many problems can open their hearts in this way, a country like Canada with its sparse population can give refuge at least to persons in the situation just referred to by the hon. member for Davenport.
Further on he said:
We are most anxious to see our country give refuge to those who have suffered, regardless of race or religion, particularly when they are relatives of persons in Canada who can
offer them a home and a new beginning in life.
As I say, that statement met with general agreement on all sides of the house, and the debates on this question and the comments made since that time have shown that the

Immigration-Displaced Persons
members of this house are anxious to contribute toward the realization of that ideal.
I should like to make a particular plea to the government in connection with the many thousands in Canada who have applied to bring their relatives to this country from displaced persons camps in Europe and in whose cases action has not yet been taken. I do not say that in any spirit of criticism, because I realize the many difficulties with which the department of immigration is faced, but I would point out that many of those who have applied have given the best assurances possible that their relatives, on arrival in Canada, will not be a charge upon this country or displace any one from work, or take up anybody else's living space, for their relatives here have made arrangements for their housing and employment and have guaranteed to look after them in case of illness or unemployment. These applicants have been waiting now in some cases for two and two and a half years, and it is difficult to keep these arrangements open indefinitely. They cannot continue to wait year after year without knowing whether their relatives in Europe will be permitted to come and what the decision of the immigration department will be. I do hope that the government can find some way to expedite the applications already on file on behalf of displaced persons for whom the best possible arrangements have been made so far as housing and employment are concerned.
#
I would emphasize that a displaced person who has a relative in Canada is probably the most desirable type of immigrant, because he will find employment and become a useful citizen immediately upon arrival. I do not believe that we are now entering into a serious era of unemployment, but there are pockets of unemployment across the country today. Naturally some people are fearful lest new arrivals may displace labour in this country, but the ones of whom I speak are assured of employment and housing and a start in life by their relatives in this country. I hope, therefore, that the government will do everything possible to expedite the consideration of these applications so that these displaced persons may find a haven and a new start in life in this great country of ours.

DISCOVERT OF POTASH DEPOSIT IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
A matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the house tonight for a few minutes is something new, and something which I think is of considerable importance. I refer to the discovery made some time ago of a potash deposit in Saskatchewan. I should like to explain to hon. members that before that discovery no potash was known to exist in Canada. The fertilizer need of Canadian soil is large and growing. I should like to point out that surveys made by the Department of Agriculture, by the men who are qualified to make them, state that the present consumption of fertilizer in western Canada is some 57,000 tons. These experts estimate that future requirements will be approximately 237,000 tons, or four times the present consumption. In 1936 the consumption of fertilizer in eastern Canada amounted to something over 215.000 tons. In 1946 the use of fertilizer had increased to 571,000 tons, or an increase of 265 per cent.
I should like to point out that the main constituents of fertilizer in Canada used by Canadian farmers are phosphates, nitrates and potash. Of these three, potash is probably of the least importance, but it is of some considerable importance. Also, since 1944 Canada used 44,000 tons of potash.
As I said a moment ago, a potash deposit was discovered in Saskatchewan. It was discovered in connection with the drilling of a gas and oil well at Unity. The deposit was eleven feet in thickness, and had an average potassium oxide content of 21-5 per cent, which compares favourably with other potash deposits being mined at the present time for commercial production in other parts of the world. Because little was known of potash mining in Canada, experts from the Saskatchewan department of national resources and the dominion bureau of mines and resources paid a visit to New Mexico to study mining methods there. It was found that in New Mexico the potash deposits occurred much nearer to the surface. It was estimated by' some.of the experts that the potash deposit in Saskatchewan was perhaps too deep for commercial development. speechtext: The rule that the hon. member has read would not apply. The estimates will be before the house; indeed, some of them are now before the house. I submit that this discussion is out of order, and that we should go on with the business of the house.

Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, and having regard to the ruling to which you have referred, I think the subject I should like to discuss for a few minutes at this time is in order, it being a matter that cannot be discussed at any time under the estimates, one which has arisen within the last few hours and one on which I should like to ask the government to take action which so far they have not indicated that they are willing to do.
I refer again to the flood situation in British Columbia; and I do so because I have just received word, through a Canadian Press dispatch headlined Vancouver, 9.11 p.m., to the effect that the Premier of British Columbia, Mr. Johnson, has declared martial law in the British Columbia flooded areas, and that he has implored the army to conscript civilians. There is another item, datelined 9.18 p.m., reporting the declaration of an emergency and calling on the local army commanders to call out all troops available in the province to assist in handling the situation. As hon. members will have seen by the press, apparently the floods are becoming worse hourly. The last actual information we had was that the Kootenay and Columbia river systems were now going on the rampage, had burst a dam and inundated some 8,000 acres of wheat land and were-I do not state this as fact but as a rumour- imperilling the Consolidated Smelters plant at Trail, British Columbia, or at least placing it under some danger.
I rise to speak on this matter now, because this afternoon, when it was raised before the orders of the day were called, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicated in a statement he made that he felt there was no reason to believe that the local authorities, the Red Cross and such other charitable and auxiliary organizations could not cope with the situation. Although I have not had a chance to see the report of his remarks in Hansard, as I recall it he went on to indicate that the present feeling of the federal government was that it was not a matter on which they should, of their own accord, take any

action; and he supported the stand in that regard set forth by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) on Friday last.
That to my mind indicates clearly that, with respect to initiating any action, the federal government have not up to the moment felt that they should do anything of the sort. Now that we have this situation growing so much worse that the premier of our province has had to take the important and serious step of declaring martial law and asking that the troops be called out-not to impose order but simply to help him handle the situation-I think that fact speaks for itself, and it must be obvious that the situation is far beyond the control of any local authority. Therefore I take this opportunity of raising the matter as a grievance, because I think it certainly would give us cause for a grievance if the government should not change their attitude. We ask that they change their attitude, that they now take the initiative in calling out the troops and in taking measures to make available, of their own accord, funds with which to buy materials for the relief of those suffering from the floods; also to make funds available to provincial and local authorities for the same purpose; and also to make supplies available.
I should like to pay tribute to what the forces are doing at the moment in the supplying of sandbags, tents and, I believe, food supplies as well in these stricken areas. But it is obvious that not only to cope with the existing situation but to rehabilitate the areas being devastated will be very expensive, and will require a great quantity of supplies. So I think the federal government should take the initiative in making funds available to assist in that work and in gathering together those supplies and sending them in the quantities in which they will be needed, as I say, to deal with the floods and to rehabilitate the areas, to drive the waters back and to divert the streams to their former channels.
Then I think the question will arise in regard to compensation for those who have lost their crops, their homes, their livestock and so on in the floods; but that will have to come up later. The request I make at the moment is that the government change its attitude. We have three ministers in the house at the moment. I wish the Prime Minister were here, but perhaps one of the hon. gentlemen who occupy the front benches at the moment will communicate with his colleagues in the government; and in view of the emergency that exists I am sure they would be willing even to have a special meeting so that we might have some assurance, if not tonight, then the

first thing 'tomorrow, in regard to what has been done and what will be the future action by this government to assist our own province to deal with this terrible emergency.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: The answer given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) today, as I understood it, was in reply to a request from the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Matthews), which in turn came from the town of Kimberley. The answer was to the effect that this government would not deal directly with the town of Kimberley or any other town or city, but that this government would deal with the provincial government through the premier of the province. Any appeal made to this government by the premier of British Columbia certainly will receive consideration and will be acted upon. That has already been demonstrated. The troops have been made available; the navy has been made available, officials of the various departments have been made available; I understand that the health department have offered their services in taking care of persons who may require medical attention, and I believe every assistance that has been asked for so far has been granted. As far as I know, nothing that has been requested through the proper channels has been denied; and I am quite sure anything that can be supplied will be forthcoming. The only suggestion made this afternoon was that requests should come from the correct source, that is through the premier of the province, and I am sure, when those requests are received, everything possible under the circumstances will be done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one coming from a different part of the country, may I take just a moment to support wholeheartedly the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Matthews), together with the appeals for British Columbia made on previous occasions by other hon. members from that province. We all know and appreciate the steps that have already been taken by the Department of National Defence, the offer made by the Department of National Health and Welfare, and anything else that may have been done by the federal government. But I want to say further that anything done by the federal government in the name of the people of Canada as a whole to assist our stricken fellow citizens in British Columbia will, I am sure, have the support of Canadians
from coast to coast. I happen to come from an area which only a short time ago suffered a flood condition which we felt to be extremely serious, but even parts of Canada that have not had this experience will, I am sure, support me when I say that in a time like this we are Canadians all and anything this government can do for the people of British Columbia, even if the cost should run into large figures, will have the support of all the people of this country.
