When we were dealing with the agriculture estimates the last time we were in committee the minister told about the interprovincial council or water board, as I believe he called it, and explained that they were acting in an advisory capacity, but that any recommendations they made which were acceptable to the four governments concerned, which I suppose would be the governments of the three prairie provinces and the dominion government would be put into operation. I believe that is correct?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: That is going a little further than I went, I think. We are not committed to get any project under way. This board is called the prairie provinces water board. It considers projects that should be recommended, and makes recommendations; but that does not compel any of the authorities to go ahead with the work.

But I believe the minister said, if this government accepted it and passed an order in council, and the province affected also passed an order in council, that would be the go-ahead signal?
Supply-Agriculture

At that time I was speaking of the division of water as among the provinces. When that is accepted and the provinces pass orders in council that will go ahead. But I assume no order in council will be passed by the federal government until we are prepared to proceed. When we pass an order in council the money will be available and we shall go ahead.

In the event of a project being undertaken after this procedure has been followed, I should like to be clear on one thing. Let us say the project was a large water storage undertaking which had to be agreed upon by all the provinces, since it had reference to a river passing through two or more of the provinces. In the storage of this large amount of water, one province might have many of its citizens affected in their property, farms and so on. or grazing land, or whatever might be wherever the lake is created to store the water. In addition, roads and other public services, even telephones lines, might be disrupted. Would the province affected in that way have to stand the whole of that cost itself, or would there be an arrangement under which that province would be reimbursed by this government and the other two provincial governments concerned?

An agreement will be drawn up between the governments concerned and this government as to what is to be done. For example, we have an order in council which has already been passed and which has been accepted by each of the provinces, which indicates that, before the federal government will proceed with any project, we must have an undertaking from the province that any lands belonging to the province which are to be flooded will be turned over to the dominion. Then there is the further undertaking that the water will be utilized, that either the province or some organization set up for the purpose will utilize the water for irrigation or power purposes. These undertakings will be given previously; and the conditions under which any particular project will be carried on will be written into the agreement. But, in so far as any works we have done up to the present are concerned, when we have flooded roads we have had to put a new road in, if that were possible. Where it has been necessary to raise grades because of the storing of water, we have raised grades. Where it has been possible to put in a bridge, we have put a bridge in.
The P.F.R.A. branch of the department?

Yes, at Valmarie, and dams which have been put in outside of Regina and elsewhere. We have taken care of any extra costs put on because of the work. In some places where railway lines have had to be changed, we have become responsible for them. We make our decision on that before we enter upon the project. If we decide that it will be too expensive we do not enter upon the project; but if we decide to go ahead with them, then we have done those things.

To be specific, what is
worrying me in connection with this is that *the Minister of Public Works has just announced that an order in council has been passed permitting the building of a bridge at Saskatchewan Landing but with conditions. One of the conditions is that the provincial government would be responsible for any damage that might occur if the bridge should be submerged by reason of the P.F.R.A. building a water storage at Tichfield, or whatever it happens to be.
It may be difficult for Saskatchewan to agree to any large water storage plan, or to pass an order in council for any large water storage project such as might be considered later on, unless the government here is prepared to give consideration to taking care of that additional cost. I think we should have some announcement in that regard.

So many things are involved before we get that far that I do not think an announcement would be of much use at this time. All I can say is that it is estimated there will be a certain cost result because of the bridge already across the Saskatchewan river south of the point in question where the dam is to be built. That area will be flooded. The railway goes across at that point. The cost of taking that bridge out of there altogether and putting the railway across somewhere else is all involved in these costs.
On the other matter, as to the bridge north of Swift Current, as I said the other night it has been estimated that if a certain dam were built-not the one the hon. member is speaking about, but another dam-to serve a little different purpose, the water would be raised only fourteen feet. And if it is raised only fourteen feet, then all that is required is a bridge to take care of that. That is what I understand the provincial government intends to build. But they are being asked to put in abutments which will carry a bridge fifty-three feet higher. And when that time comes,

if we were going to build the dam I imagine there would be some cost which would have to be taken care of as part of the costs of putting in water storage. But as to what part it would be, I am not in a position to say; and I do not think anyone can say. There would be some part of the cost of raising the bridge, of putting it at a different level, which would probably have to be taken care of as part of the expense of doing the construction.
By all concerned?
Yes.

I should like to add something to what has been said with respect to water storage on the Saskatchewan river and the use of that basin's water for the two main purposes of irrigation and power.
I would judge, from what has been said by the minister, that the program as to what is to be carried out is not yet in definite form, and in my opinion that is all to the good. It is a big job, and it will have to be surveyed from every angle. Having covered most of the great rivers in western America which have been put under control for irrigation and power purposes, I can also say I have covered the Saskatchewan river. Five different trips were required to do the full job, and these were taken in as many recesses of parliament. During those recesses I did cover the river from its main source in the Columbia glacier right down to Grand Rapids. I do not. mean I traversed every step of the river; but I investigated every pertinent area which had anything to do with flood controls, water conservation or irrigation.
Across the line they have followed the very same procedure and have set up a good program or a series of programs in connection with their control over their great rivers. I, myself, thoroughly surveyed the Platte river basin from its source in the mountains to its mouth where it pours into the Missouri river. The Missouri river program is not yet complete, but I have covered most of that part which is complete.
It starts in the Rocky mountains and flows into the Mississippi. I did the same in connection with the Colorado river, one of the great rivers of America, from where it rises in the southern part of Wyoming, Utah and northern Colorado right down to a point below Boulder dam, where the river flows between California and Arizona.	In like
manner I have investigated the Salt river valley in Arizona from its source in the mountains.
So I feel I have had some little experience in these problems. In each of those basins, the basin is under an authority. I have in mind the Tennessee valley authority, which I thoroughly surveyed from beginning to end. It was the first valley to have an authority. It was ten years or more ago, after the defeat of the Bennett government. I do not recall exactly whether the minister was in the house at that time, but if he was he will recall my proposing to the house that we should have a Saskatchewan river authority, so that there would be a unified program agreed upon by the different departments having to do with this matter in the three western provinces, in association with the federal government.
In the United States that is all under control of the bureau of reclamation. But its program is laid out after consultation with the very states through which the rivers flow. For instance, in connection with the Colorado river the conference takes place between Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, California and Arizona; and I believe one source in and of the river also touches the west of New Mexico. There are six or seven states in all.
In respect of the Tennessee river, it was a conference of seven states, through which the Tennessee flows or the boundaries of which it touches. In respect of the Platte river the states of Colorado, Wyoming and Nebraska were involved. The same program is now in operation in connection with the Columbia river which, I might say, has the greatest flow of any river in the United States with the exception of the Mississippi. It is a very great river indeed.
That is what this board is for.

I am glad to hear that. Perhaps it has not come to fruition yet; but if the minister follows that program, a program similar to that followed by the bureau of reclamation, he will be on eminently safe ground, because each of those states has its own rights and privileges, the same as our provinces would have. In a conference you would decide how much of the flow would belong to each of the provinces in the west. In our case I would say approximately ninety per cent of the flow comes from Alberta. At Fort a la Corne I believe the average volume is about 56,000,000 tons per twenty-four hours, or something between 27,000 and 30,000 cubic feet per second.
The North Saskatchewan and South Saskatchewan have not the same flow. At Cole rapids the average flow of the North Saskat-
Supply-Agriculture

chewan is about 9,500 cubic feet per second, while at Saskatoon the average flow of the South Saskatchewan is about 11,000 cubic feet per second. The South Saskatchewan has the larger flow of the two rivers.
While it may not come under this vote, I think I should compliment the minister upon what he is doing on the St. Mary river. There he is following the program carried out in the United States and, as I have often recommended, of commencing conservation operations at the headwaters of all the source branches of the main river. I should think the board or authority set up to take charge of the Saskatchewan river basin should plan along the same lines as those followed in the United States. It should try to do on the other headwaters of the Saskatchewan river what you are now doing on the St. Mary river.
There are at least twenty-four splendid reservoir sites at the headwaters of the North Saskatchewan and at least six on the South Saskatchewan. There are more than that, but I have not seen the others. All those sites should be included in the final basin program for the conservation of that water. Water is the second most priceless resource of the prairie provinces. The first is land, but neither the one nor the other is worth anything unless they are both included in a program of conservation.
The land in the west has all the required chemicals to produce the food necessary for the maintenance of peace in the world. With a minimum rainfall of about ten inches, the water requirements of the whole basin can be met if conserved as outlined. The volume of water here is not the same by any means to be found in the United States rivers. In Salt river basin in Arizona they are able to provide three to five feet per acre. I doubt if they could raise any crops there without that water, but even with that amount they cannot raise any more in that hot climate than is raised in Alberta with a minimum of eighteen inches of irrigation water per acre, and even that is not always available.
I have made a careful study of the effects of water in southern Alberta. I learn that until July, 1947, they had average moisture conditions, but in July it went down to as low as -21 inches of rainfall. That amount of rain is almost worthless. During the summer time they had only a flow of about 400 to 500 cubic feet per second from the St. Mary river, but with that they were able to produce about $85,000,000 worth of crops and livestock. If they had had all the water they should have had with a normal rainfall of about ten

inches, they would have been able to produce crops of two more bushels of wheat to the acre than they did, or twenty bushels per acre.
The program the minister has in view will provide water, and I for one am going to support it as strongly as I can. We should store the water that God has given this western country. As I say, I have seen many good reservoir sites, at the cost of a great deal of exertion, particularly those on the North Saskatchewan. There is the large and splendid site at the gap and another one at the whirlpool, and twenty-five or more others, each of which could store a large volume of water. I am speaking from memory, but I believe I am safe in saying that there could be stored on the whole Saskatchewan river basin, mostly within Alberta, approximately 30,000,000 acre feet of water, water which now runs away to melt ice in Hudson bay.
I am glad the minister has taken hold of this project. If he is long enough in office, which I cannot say he should be-as long as he is in- office, I for one will support this program to survey thoroughly and conserve the priceless water resources of the Saskatchewan river for use for irrigation and power.
If my memory serves me correctly, there could be developed, if the water is judiciously used, 5,000,000 horsepower more or less from the source to the mouth of the river. That is a lot of power. That would include the diversion of the river at Cedar lake, down through lake Winnipegosis and lake Manitoba. A very large amount of power can be developed where the diverted river would fall into lake Winnipeg at Dauphin river.
From my point of view it does not matter how much money the government must have to conserve the water on this watershed and to use it properly. As I said a few moments ago, in southern Alberta below Lethbridge, where only 250,000 or 300,000 acres are partly irrigated with approximately eighteen inches of water per acre, they were able to produce in 1947 $85,000,000 of new wealth. That would never have been produced without even that -minimum amount of water. They are not getting maximum amounts like they do in Arizona.
The program the minister has envisioned is a gigantic one. It may cost 8100 million, or perhaps $200 million, with the power development. On the basis "of a 20-year program that means approximately $10,000,000 a year. That would be simply an investment; it would not be a charge at all.
I do not want to prolong this discussion. In a word this covers what I have in mind

Supply-Agriculture
about the Saskatchewan river. This is a gigantic profit-making program, and I am willing to support such a program which will be for the benefit of Canada.

I listened with great interest to the discussion of the hon. member for Davenport and I am in agreement with his views respecting the great possibilities and potentialities connected with power development on the western plains. But I do not share with him quite the optimism with which he views the immediate future and the probability of this development taking place, in view' of the agreement entered into as between the provinces and the dominion.
I am very much in favour of the setting up of a water power board. It is necessary by reason of the divided jurisdiction between the provinces and the dominion covering the development of our natural resources. But order in council P.C. 2413 in my belief may well postpone indefinitely or for many years to come any development in connection with irrigation in Saskatchewan. I point out this, and I wish the minister would deal with it at some length. In the preamble to the order in council these words appear in paragraph 3:
And whereas in view of representations received from the provinces concerned it is now considered desirable that any recommendations of the board should become effective only upon ratification by the two or more provinces concerned and by Canada;
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture and the Acting Minister of Mines and Resources, is pleased, hereby, to approve the revised form of agreement, of which a copy is hereto attached.
Apparently some negotiations have gone on between the provinces and the dominion in the past two years in regard to this matter, and I would suggest to the minister that, in order to clarify the meaning of that portion of the order in council, he table in the house and make part of the proceedings of the house the reports or correspondence which have passed between the several provinces and the dominion with respect to this matter.
To this order in council is attached an agreement which I have in my hand. It provides for the setting up of a board to be known as the prairie provinces water board, to be composed of five members, two to be appointed by the governor general in council, and one by the lieutenant governor in council in each of the provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Its functions are set forth, and those functions are mainly administrative, to collate and analyse the data now available relating to the water and associated resources of interprovincial streams with respect to their utiliz-tion for irrigation, drainage, storage, power, industrial, municipal, navigation and other purposes. Those powers are merely administrative powers.
The essence of the agreement is this:
Upon the request of any one of the three provinces or the dominion to recommend the allocation of the waters of any interprovincial stream among the respective provinces.
In other words, the power of this board is restricted to the administrative job of collating the information and finally, upon the request of the dominion or the provinces, recommending the allocation of the waters.
I try to picture the situation-each of the provinces jealous of its own rights and powers, each of the provinces anxious to conserve as much as possible the waters that would ordinarily flow through its territory. Well, a recommendation is made, and then the trouble begins, because section 5 of the agreement reads:
A recommendation of the board with respect to any matters referred to it under subsections c and d of section 4 hereof

One of those has to do with the allocation of the waters.
-shall become effective when adopted by orders in council passed by Canada and by each of the provinces affected thereby.
I fully realize the difficulties in getting an agreement with the provinces, but we have all had experience in recent years of the emasculating effect of the veto.
How would you propose to get around it?
I am just pointing out the difficulty at the moment. The effect of that is this, that nothing can be done without unanimity.
Oh, no.

I will read the section again:
A recommendation of the hoard with respect to any matters referred to it under subsections c and d of section 4 hereof shall become effective when adopted by orders in, council passed by Canada and by each of the provinces affected thereby.
The minister says that is not the effect, that it does not require unanimity, that any one province may not apply the veto. I say to him this: that is the way I read it; that is the way it is drafted; that is the purport of that section of the agreement in its present form. The minister asks: How are you going to get around that? I realize the difficulty, but I would point out this-
Supply-Agriculture
That is what they did on the Colorado.

Yes, and it cannot be done in any other way. That is what is being done on the St. Mary river now. We must, before some particular time, take advantage of the fact that this water is allotted to us, and that is why we are building the dam at this moment on the St. Mary river to store up the water to which we have a right as a result of the decision of the international joint commission. This board will operate in exactly the same way. There is nobody going to sit down and veto things like the Russian government. The provinces will be anxious to have the money spent in their respective provinces. They will be anxious to have the work done.

If they are so
anxious, they would not have asked for the powers of veto.
They did not ask for the powers of veto. They refused to have an order in council with the power of veto in it.
All right; let me complete my argument. The very fact that the minister immediately jumps before I get even part of the way indicates that I have touched a point of pronounced interest.

No, it does not indicate that at all; it indicates that the hon. member is trying to put up a theory which does not exist, and talk until eleven o'clock so that it is given publicity over the country and goes out that way. It just cannot go out that way in view of what I have said.

I say to the minister that if he has a plan for the expenditure of $110 million that is today being dangled before the western provinces, why did he not submit that plan to the provinces and secure their agreement to that expenditure, provided that it could be proven efficacious.
That plan was submitted to the provinces two years ago.

That is fine. If it was submitted to the provinces two years ago, why is it that they are not prepared to accept the plan that was submitted to them? If it has been submitted to them, then we already know that plan has not been accepted by each of the provinces.

No; the point is this. We did not assume the position that we have all the knowledge on the matter. We submitted to the provinces the plan which they thought they could improve upon. We have accepted some of their suggestions and put them in the form of this resolution.

In order to clarify the whole situation, I am pointing out that if the people of western Canada believe that the plan which the minister has placed before them could be carried into effect without the consent of the provinces they are due to be undeceived.
They are not being asked to do that; they are going to consent.
Placed before this house and the country.

I appreciate the
general plan, but I want to see how it was placed before the provinces. Certainly, as far as this house is concerned, what was placed before it was merely a generality. I wish the

minister would table the correspondence passed between the provinces and the dominion on this matter-

May I point out to my hon. friend that a considerable part of it is right in front of him, and he is discussing it under an item under which he is not entitled to discuss it at all. The whole plan is enunciated in the items that are recited, one being this very item, but part of it is covered in the next item, the St. Mary river dam project, which is already under way, and a very considerable part of it constructed. Then you go on down through the items and you find parts of it on the next page. The items have already been dealt with session after session. If you take the items which are mentioned in No. 30 and add them to the St. Mary river dam project it will amount to SI 10 million.
.Mr. DIEFENBAKER:	I am directing my
attention at the moment to the general scheme which has been brought to the attention of the people of Saskatchewan. That scheme will cost approximately $66,000,000.
That is one of the projects.

What we have
before us under item 30 amounts to 13,000,000 in 1948-49, and item No. 31, the St. Mary river dam project, amounts to $2,200,000.

In the projects that are here, there are: the Medicine Hat irrigation scheme, which is $4,000,000; the Red Deer diversion project, which runs somewhere between $15,000,000 and $20,000,000; the South Saskatchewan river project, which is $66,000,000. These items together will come very close to what is being proposed, and then there is the St. Mary river dam project, which will cost $15,000,000 to $20,000,000. These total up to around $110 million. The whole program is right in front of the hon. member.
Merely a survey of these various projects.
They have to be surveyed first.

I am asking the minister this simple question. Our people are being led to believe that within a couple of years a great construction proposition will be undertaken in our province, provided that it is proven by surveys to be efficacious and efficient.
And provided that the province is prepared to go on with the development.
Yes, we have that veto. It still rests with the province.
It is not a veto at all. It is whether they want to spend the money, that is all.

So that we can get this out of the sphere of a more or less ephemeral promise or the expectation of a hope, I am asking the minister to table the correspondence regarding the particular matter, and I am not going outside my own province. All I am asking for at the moment is the correspondence that passed between his department, or any other department of government, and the governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba respecting the river projects in Saskatchewan.

I will answer that by saying that every bit of discussion and correspondence, and the forms in connection with it, have already been tabled in this house. The main part of it is the report of the engineers, and that has been a matter of discussion as between the province and ourselves. We have spent the money with regard to it, and we have the report. We have put the report on the table of the house. We have said to the provinces, Are you prepared to proceed with the development of irrigation or power as a result of the building of the dam, if it is built?
Are these questions in writing?

These discussions have all taken place, most of them orally as between the governments, but everything of importance in connection with the matter is in writing. It is set down, and it has all been placed on the table of the house.
